description.narrative: Denmark’s Foreign and Security Policy Strategy (2022) reiterates that stabilisation measures serve Danish interests at home and abroad, especially “to prevent attacks against local populations, irregular migration flows, and extremism as well as to ensure the rights of women.” Accordingly, the partnership with UNODC will focus on addressing transboundary and evolving threats in the Horn of Africa with an emphasis on those that destabilize Somalia, including the Federal Government of Somalia’s (FGS) ability to combat illicit goods from which terrorist and transnational organized crime groups generate revenue. Among other activities, UNODC will assist the FGS in protecting its territorial borders and complying with United Nations sanctions. Importantly, UNODC will mainstream gender and aspects of the Women, Peace & Security Agenda into its various activities and actively identify/rectify gaps, with a view to empowering women to play a more prominent role in peace and security.

title.narrative: Output 1.2 Facilitate and support inter agency coordination in Kenya and Somalia to enhance the management of maritime and land borders for the disruption of illicit trade from which violent extremist organisations and transnational organised crime groups profit.
Communications activities or materials are developed to raise awareness among Kenyan border communities of the adverse effects of illicit trade, including the effects on vulnerable groups.

target.value: Enable leaders of two target border communities to facilitate townhalls and raise awareness among locals of the consequences of illicit trade, including its association with peace and security.

actual.value:
Due to security situation within the border areas ( Kenya-Somalia border of Garissa and Mandera) all year, the region was not cleared for conducting the sensitization training and townhalls for raising awareness among locals on the consequences of illicit trade. However, plans are in motion to have these sensitization trainings held in 2024.
In the first half of 2023, with regards focus area one of the Kenya roadmap, UNODC sensitized 20 Lamu-based community leaders to the adverse economic, social, and security effects of illicit trade. Barazas (town halls) were subsequently led by trained community leaders to enable wider community outreach.
In October 2023, UNODC facilitated the participation of 6 KCGS officers in the Advanced Training of Trainers course. The Advanced TOT course, which was conducted by the Danish National Police, is an effort under its peace and stabilization programme IV to create conditions for longer term stability through the training of officers in the reg

target.value: Enable leaders of two more target border communities to facilitate townhalls and raise awareness among locals of the consequences of illicit trade, including its association with peace and security.

actual.value: In August 2024, UNODC GMCP in partnership with the Kenya Border Management Secretariat held two sensitization workshops in Wajir and Garissa for moret than 100 residents, community leaders, and traders led by the Assistant County Commissioner to introduce the topic of Combating Illicit Trade and Its Effects Along the Kenya Somalia Border. Discussions covered the impact of illicit trade on health and the economy, links between illicit trade and terrorism detection of illicit goods, community roles in investigations, and regulatory sanctions.

target.value: Border communities are aware of the security, economic, and health implications caused by illicit trade.

actual.value: In October 2025, Kenyas Counter Terrorism Police Unit arrested eight Al Shabaab operatives in Garissa following actionable intelligence provided by local community members. The suspects were in the process of attempting to assemble improvised explosive devices IEDs in the WelmererYumbia area, and their arrest prevented a potentially deadly attack. In November 2025, further community generated intelligence enabled a multi agency counter terrorism team to intercept additional suspected terrorists attempting to cross into Kenya from Somalia through Garissa County. These incidents underscore the critical role of community engagement and outreach in counter terrorism efforts. By strengthening trust and encouraging the reporting of suspicious activities, community based approaches significantly enhance early warning, disrupt terrorist operations, and contribute to improved security, stability, and economic resilience across the Horn of Africa.

target.value: Community leaders continue the sensitization efforts independently from international support with monitoring and coordination by the Border Management Secretariat.

title.narrative: Violent extremist organizations (VEOs) and transnational organized crime networks influence and their means of gaining revenue and capabilities in the Horn of Africa on land and sea are diminished.
The beneficiaries can sustain the continuation of the handed over frameworks, with subsequent monitoring of activities post-programme where relevant.

target.value: Enhanced capacities enable greater cooperation to disrupt the flow of illicit goods across the land and maritime borders and reduce funding for violent extremist organizations in the Horn of Africa.

actual.value:
In 2024, a range of activities were carried out to advance the overall project objective, including:
Delivery of Maritime Law Enforcement and advanced mentoring and training Concluded research and analysis on the resurgence of piracy in the Gulf of Aden, Red Sea and Horn of Africa region. Finalization of plans on FGS/FMS engagement in support of the roadmap to combat illicit trade along Somalia-Kenya-Ethiopia border. Bolstered research and analysis on breaches of the sanctions regime in connection with illicit maritime flows and transnational organized crime networks. Engagement with Kenya on MLE capacity building, and Kenya-Somalia coordinated border management

target.value: Enhanced capacities enable greater cooperation to disrupt the flow of illicit goods across the land and maritime borders and reduce funding for violent extremist organizations in the Horn of Africa.

actual.value: In this reporting period, the project recorded substantial progress toward its overarching goals, particularly in building institutional capacity, strengthening interagency cooperation, and advancing gender inclusion within maritime and border security frameworks. Several key results were achieved that collectively enhanced the effectiveness and inclusivity of security operations along the Kenya Somalia border and beyond: Strengthened Interdictions and Disruption of Transnational Maritime Crime As a direct outcome of the project targeted interventions and sustained capacity building efforts, Kenya and Somalia achieved multiple successful interdictions over the reporting year across a spectrum of serious maritime and transnational crimes. These results were particularly impactful in countering terrorism in the Horn of Africa, where enhanced operational coordination, joint tasking, and improved information sharing enabled national authorities to more effectively disrupt terrorist and criminal networks along Kenya Somalia border. Beyond counterterrorism, the strengthened capabilities of supported agencies translated into tangible gains against drug trafficking, human trafficking, and piracy. Improved maritime law enforcement across sea, port, and border domains increased deterrence, enhanced regional security, and demonstrated the growing ability of national institutions to respond coherently and effectively to complex crossborder threats. Strengthened Gender Inclusion in Maritime Law Enforcement: The successful convening of the Women in the Maritime Sector Workshops have resulted in increased visibility and participation of females in the in maritime sector. Integrated Information Management Capabilities: To complement the Information Management and Sharing (IMS) training previously delivered to frontline border officers along the Kenya Somalia border, an advanced IMS curriculum tailored for senior level officers from Kenya and Somalia was developed in the quarters. This initiative seeks to equip leadership with the strategic tools needed to align information practices with coordinated border management objectives and to drive organizational change. Advancing Regional Maritime and Border Security During the reporting period, the project achieved significant progress in enhancing regional maritime and border security by reinforcing international mandates, boosting multilateral coordination, and strengthening national ownership in both Somalia and Kenya. By improving policy frameworks, fostering interagency collaboration, and aligning with regional and global security priorities, the initiative enabled more integrated and effective responses to transnational crime, terrorism, and maritime threats, ultimately contributing to greater stability and security across the region. Collectively, these achievements reflect meaningful progress toward the project strategic outcomes, with measurable improvements in coordination, capacity, and inclusivity across maritime and border law enforcement agencies.

target.value: Enhanced capacities enable greater cooperation to disrupt the flow of illicit goods across the land and maritime borders and reduce funding for violent extremist organizations in the Horn of Africa.

title.narrative: Outcome 1 Somalia and Kenya have greater capacity to facilitate and apply regional cooperation for enhanced control over maritime and land borders to diminish violent extremist organisations, while also ensuring mainstreaming women, peace and security to limit VEO's ability to benefit from illicit trade.
Somali and Kenya border agencies overcome challenges to disrupt illicit trade from which violent extremist organisations profit.

target.value: Increased number of trained officers in Somalia and Kenya has enabled greater information exchanges across government, in border communities, and UNODC to inform responses to evolving cross-border threats, ensuring a gendered lens is embedded as a cross-cutting priority.

actual.value: In Somalia, the maritime law enforcement units in Berbera patrol operations average around 24 hours/week including night patrol which is 96 hours/month. In Bossaso, the maritime law enforcement units patrol 65 hours/week using 3 skiffs and 8 personnel per skiff and averaging 260 hours/month. In Mogadishu, the maritime law enforcement units patrol 35 hours/week, which is 140 hours/month. During this reporting period, over 76 officers at each location received training in maritime law enforcement, Maritime Domain Awareness, and marine communications. In July 2024, the UNODC Global Maritime Crime Programme (GMCP), in partnership with the Danish National Police, organized an advanced Training of Trainers (ToT) course for officers from the Kenya Coast Guard Service (KCGS), the Kenya Navy, and the East African Standby Force. This initiative focused on enhancing the participants' instructional skills and expertise while fostering the creation of comprehensive training plans customized to meet the specific needs of their respective agencies. The program aimed to promote sustainable capacity building in maritime security and law enforcement, empowering these organizations to address emerging challenges effectively and independently. In September and December 2024, UNODC GMCP conducted a Basic Instructor Course for forty participants from the Kenya Coast Guard Service (KCGS) and the Border Management Secretariat. This initiative is a collaborative effort with two instructors from the Danish National Police and was supported by three national instructors from the KCGS. The course was designed to provide participants with the fundamental skills required to become national instructors. Participants engaged in practical exercises, gaining hands-on experience in delivering presentations, facilitating group discussions, and evaluating student learning outcomes. By the conclusion of the course, participants possessed the confidence and expertise needed to teach effectively and mentor others within their respective fields.

target.value: Increased number of trained officers in Somalia and Kenya has enabled greater information exchanges across government, in border communities, and UNODC to inform responses to evolving cross-border threats, ensuring a gendered lens is embedded as a cross-cutting priority.

actual.value: Maritime law enforcement units in Berbera conduct patrols averaging 24 hours per week, including night patrols, totaling about 96 hours per month. In Bossaso, units patrol about 65 hours per week using three skiffs with eight personnel per skiff, totaling about 260 hours per month. From 24 to 28 July 2025, a multi agency training programme strengthened information management and inter agency cooperation in Somalias maritime sector. Eighteen participants from the Federal Government and Federal Member States, including Customs, Coast Guard, Ministry of Ports, Ministry of Fisheries, and Criminal Investigation Department, learned structured communication frameworks, best practices for maritime information systems, and scenario based exercises to improve coordinated responses to maritime threats. On 28 July, UNODC GMCP concluded a similar multi agency training supported by instructors from the Kenya Coast Guard Service, reinforcing collaborative data sharing and coordinated maritime governance among the same group of Somali institutions. From 25 to 29 August 2025, UNODC GMCP delivered an Information Management and Sharing training course in Mombasa for 18 officers from the Kenya Coast Guard Service and the Border Management Secretariat. The course, led by certified national trainers, strengthened inter agency cooperation and the ability to collect, analyze, and share operational information across sea, land, and air domains, while promoting national ownership of training capacity. From 27 to 31 October 2025, UNODC GMCP with support from the Danish National Police delivered an IMS curriculum development course for instructors from the Kenya Coast Guard Service, the Border Management Secretariat, and the Bosasso Port Maritime Police Unit. The course produced an advanced senior level officer module focused on complex information analysis, leadership in multi agency operations, and inclusive leadership principles, with immediate rollout planned in Kenya and Somalia. From 3 to 7 November 2025, a senior level IMS course in Mombasa trained 20 participants from the Kenya Coast Guard Service, Border Management Secretariat, Bosasso Port Maritime Police Unit, Somali Police Force Department of Coast Guard, and Somalia Police. Delivered by national instructors with technical support from the Danish National Police, the training enhanced strategic and operational information sharing, decision making, risk management, and cross border coordination.

title.narrative: Output 2.1 Monitor the Garowe Central Prison and the Mogadishu Prison and Court Complex to ensure prisoners are held in conditions that comply with international human right standards.
SOPs and policy documents are updated based on the recommendations resulting from the IMC and National Prison Monitoring Committee reporting.

target.value: SOPs are updated based on the number of recommendations and meetings held by the IMC and National Prison Monitoring Committee.

actual.value: On 17 September 2023, there was a UN coordinated visit to Garowe prison. The purpose of the visit was to understand the needs of Garowe Prison to strengthen its operational capacity to meet the diverse needs of prisoners with a focus on human rights, identify gaps, and recommend appropriate interventions.

target.value: The prisons monitored use on day-to-day activity the SOPs and recommendation from the IMC and National Prison Monitoring Committee visits.

actual.value: On 22 July, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime Global Maritime Crime Programme and Banadir University held a workshop to strengthen psychosocial support in prisons. The session built prison staff capacity to foster trust, support behaviour change, and promote communication skills to enable more humane and rehabilitative incarceration and reintegration. On 23 July, the programme conducted a mentoring session at the Mogadishu Prison and Court Complex to improve vocational training integration and prepare for infrastructure development under the Joint Justice and Corrections Programme funded by the European Union and the Government of the Netherlands. Vocational training graduates contributed to constructing a new operations office, demonstrating how skills based rehabilitation can improve infrastructure while building employable skills. On 11 October, the programme completed a two day training in Mogadishu for 56 correctional officers, co facilitated by national trainers. The course covered humane treatment, stress management, security practices, reintegration, relapse prevention, and Nonviolent Communication based on Marshall Rosenberg framework. Through practical exercises and structured feedback methods, officers strengthened communication, leadership, and human rights competencies for professional custodial practice.

target.value: SOPs developed on the management of violent extremist prisoners and female prisoners, specifically aligned with the recommendations from the IMC visit.
At the Federal Member States, the Somali Custodial Corps and MOJCA create SOPs and policy documents based on the recommendations formulated during the visits.

title.narrative: Outcome 2: The National Prison Monitoring Committee can sustain the human rights monitoring at target prison with a community monitoring mechanism.

Outcome Indicator: The National Prison Monitoring Committee uses the human right checklist and prepares reports with the support of UNODCs prison experts to maintain the independence of the assessments.

target.value: The National Prison Monitoring Committee hosts monitoring missions and prepares assessment reports based on a checklist prepared with UNODC and its prison experts.

actual.value:
On 7 August, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime Global Maritime Crime Programme conducted a monitoring visit to Garowe Prison, reviewing female and juvenile wards, overall conditions, access to services, hygiene standards, and rehabilitation programmes. The visit identified gaps and provided guidance to improve daily operations, protect vulnerable inmates, and strengthen corrections management. Findings will inform future support to improve infrastructure, living standards, and access to education and vocational training.
On 22 August, the programme visited Hargeisa Prison and met partners including United Nations Development Programme Rule of Law, the High Commissioner, and the Prison Commander to strengthen collaboration under the Joint Rule of Law Programme, assess prison management practices, and identify opportunities to enhance staff capacity and inmate conditions.
On 12 October, a monitoring and evaluation visit to the Mogadishu Prison Court Complex and Mogadishu Prison assessed vocational and training programmes where inmates are actively refurbishing facilities. The visit highlighted how skills based training is improving safety, infrastructure, and rehabilitation outcomes while building practical, marketable skills that support reintegration and strengthen the corrections system in Somalia.

target.value: The National Prison Monitoring Committee hosts monitoring missions and prepares assessment reports based on a checklist prepared by UNODC.
